appr1-thy-estimation.reason: Opens on the vow frame; why the numbers were published (to take power from whoever names them) and why the mercy (verse 8 shows the figure measures the obligation, not the man) come mid-lesson; ends on right vs favour.
appr1-thy-estimation.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why did Yahweh publish the numbers and still make room for mercy? He published them so the power to name a figure would not sit with the stronger party, and the weak could check what they were asked. He wrote the mercy into the same law so a poor man could ask for it as a right, not hope for it as a favour. And the mercy proves the figures never priced a person. Here is how Leviticus 27 shows it.
appr1-thy-estimation.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why publish the numbers and still make room for mercy? Because each protects the person with less power. The published schedule means no one can invent a figure at the door (Leviticus 27:3, 7). The mercy, written beside it at the same authority, lets the poor man present himself and be valued by his ability (Leviticus 27:8). Since poverty can lower the figure, it was never measuring his worth, only his vow. A steward can copy both tomorrow: name your figures openly, and make your mercy a right people can ask for.

teen.open: Why did Yahweh write the prices down for everyone to see, and then let poor people pay less? So no one could be cheated by a made-up number, and so the poor had a real right to ask for mercy.
teen.close: So why both? Clear numbers protect the weak from being cheated, and mercy in the law means the poor can ask without begging. The price was for a promise, never for a person.

senior.open: The title asks why Yahweh published the figures and yet made room for mercy. Publication takes the power to name a price away from the stronger party, and the written mercy makes relief a right rather than a kindness.
senior.close: So the answer is this. The open schedule guards against invented prices, and the provision for the poor, at the same authority, lets a man ask by right. That the figure can bend for poverty shows it measured the vow, never the worth of the man.

appr3-according-to-the-years-that-remain.reason: Value-from-yield appears early, but the title's answer (you pay for the harvests left before the land returns, not the dirt) is only stated near the end; closes on method, not the reader's price.
appr3-according-to-the-years-that-remain.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What are you really paying for when you buy a property? Not the dirt. You are paying for the harvests, the use, you will actually receive before it goes back or wears out. Leviticus 27 values a field by its seed, what it can produce, and then reduces the price by the years that remain before the jubilee. Your price hides the years. Here is how the law brings them into the open.
appr3-according-to-the-years-that-remain.example: EIGHT YEARS OF ROOF. Say you are buying a house whose roof has eight of its twenty-five years left. The instinct is to price a roof. But what changes hands is eight years of shelter from that roof, not twenty-five. The same goes for a lease with a term, a machine with a service life, or a business whose largest customer has three years to run. Ask each time: how much use remains, and when does it end?
appr3-according-to-the-years-that-remain.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What are you really paying for? The years of yield you will receive, never the ground itself. The law starts from what a field produces (Leviticus 27:16), and then reckons the money by the years that remain until the jubilee (Leviticus 27:18). It is calculated, not haggled, by someone with no stake, from a published base to a known end. Price the use that remains, show your working to both sides, and your price stops hiding what you are actually buying.

teen.open: When you buy land or a house, what are you really paying for? Not the ground. You are paying for what it will give you before it goes back or wears out.
teen.close: So what are you really buying? The years of use left. Count them honestly, and you will pay a fair price.

senior.open: The title asks what you truly pay for in a property. Leviticus 27 answers: the harvests you will receive before the land returns, priced by its yield and reduced by the years that remain.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. You were never buying the dirt but the years of use left to you. The law computes that openly, from a known base to a known end, which is the honest way to price anything with a term.

appr4-he-shall-add-the-fifth-part.reason: Makes the fifth concrete at once, but why it ends negotiation and why the redemption window closes (Lev 27:20-21) come late; the closing pairing is stated, then drifts into a warning about rights with no end.
appr4-he-shall-add-the-fifth-part.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does paying a fixed fifth more make the deal stop being negotiable, and why can the window to buy back close? Because the added twenty per cent never changes, there is nothing to bargain over, and leaning on the valuer for a low figure stops paying. And the right to redeem is real, so it can really lapse: the law itself says when. Here is what Leviticus 27 shows.
appr4-he-shall-add-the-fifth-part.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does a fixed fifth end the negotiation, and why can the window close? The same fifth applies to a house, a field and a tithe (Leviticus 27:15, 19, 31), so the forceful man gains nothing and the timid man loses nothing. The text does not give the reason; we teach only what the fifth does. And the right expires: a field not redeemed is not redeemed any more (Leviticus 27:20-21). The fixed fraction makes the price unarguable. The stated end makes the clock visible to both sides.

teen.open: Why did buying something back always cost one-fifth more, with no haggling? So nobody could push for a better deal. And the chance to buy it back had a real deadline.
teen.close: So the answer: a fixed extra means no arguing, and a stated deadline means everyone can see the clock. Don't miss your window.

senior.open: The title asks why a fixed added fifth removes negotiation and why the redemption window may close. The unvarying fraction leaves nothing to bargain, and the law states plainly when the right ends.
senior.close: So the answer stands. The fifth, the same for every person and every kind of property, makes the price unarguable, and the stated expiry makes the time limit visible to both parties, rather than kept in one man's pocket.

appr2-whether-it-be-good-or-bad.reason: Answers early from Lev 27:14 (the priest, not the owner, estimates, good or bad, and it stands), but ends on the tithe of the herd and verse 33, so the reader does not finish on who values the house.
appr2-whether-it-be-good-or-bad.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who gets to say what your house is worth? One valuer with nothing to gain, not you (Leviticus 27:14). He must say what is true in both directions, good or bad, including what nobody wants written down. And his one estimate stands, so you do not go shopping until someone gives you the kinder number you had already settled on. What you transact, you appraise carefully and honestly. That is how the price comes out true for both sides.

teen.open: Who should say what a house is worth? Not the owner. Someone with nothing to gain, who tells the good and the bad.
teen.close: So who decides? A fair person with no stake, and you accept the honest answer instead of asking around until someone says what you want to hear.

senior.open: The title asks who has the right to value your house. Leviticus 27:14 answers: someone other than the owner, who speaks to its condition good or bad, and whose estimate stands.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. The honest valuer has nothing to gain, speaks in both directions, and is not replaced by a friendlier one. Seeking until a kinder figure appears is the quiet dishonesty this law closes off.

appr5-twenty-gerahs-shall-be-the-shekel.reason: Fixing the unit is shown early, but how the shrinking measure robs (Ezek 45:9-10) comes mid-lesson and the built-in check the title promises (Ezek 45:11) only in the last lines.
appr5-twenty-gerahs-shall-be-the-shekel.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does a shrinking measure rob you with no visible theft? Every printed price stays the same while the unit underneath it gets smaller, so you pay the same number for less. Nobody can point at a lie. Yahweh's answer is to fix the unit by law (twenty gerahs to the shekel), set it again when it drifts, and build the measures so each one can check the others. Here is how the Word does it.
appr5-twenty-gerahs-shall-be-the-shekel.example: THE SAME PRICE, A SMALLER BASKET. Say a basket of grain is priced the same as last year, and the receipt looks identical. But the basket now holds five per cent less. No price was raised. No one said a false word. Yet everyone who buys it loses five per cent, every time, with nothing on paper to show it. That is why the lesson says the unit is the price.
appr5-twenty-gerahs-shall-be-the-shekel.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does a shrinking measure rob you, and what check did Yahweh build in? It robs by changing what the number means while the number stays put, which is why Ezekiel lists drifting measures beside violence and extortion (Ezekiel 45:9-10). The remedy is to fix the unit (Leviticus 27:25), fix it again when it drifts (Ezekiel 45:12), and build the dry and liquid measures to one proportion of the homer, so each checks the other (Ezekiel 45:11). An ordinary person can then audit the system without trusting the man holding the vessel.

teen.open: How can someone cheat you without changing the price? By quietly making the measure smaller. Yahweh fixed the measures by law and made them check each other.
teen.close: So how do you catch it? Ask what the number is measuring, not just what it says. Yahweh designed measures that check each other, so ordinary people could spot the cheat.

senior.open: The title asks how a shrinking measure robs without visible theft, and what check Yahweh built in. The printed price holds while the unit shrinks; the remedy is a fixed unit, re-fixed when it drifts, with measures that check one another.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A drifting unit robs as surely as open extortion, which is why Ezekiel names it in the same breath. Yahweh fixed the shekel, restated it, and built the measures to one proportion so anyone could check them.

appr6-the-balances-of-deceit.reason: The scale that lies without words is explained mid-lesson; why Yahweh names the appetite (pressure can be relieved, an appetite must be repented of) arrives near the end, which then closes on an exercise warning.
appr6-the-balances-of-deceit.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How can a scale lie without a word, and why does Yahweh expose the appetite behind it? A false balance does the lying, so a merchant can be polite and accurate in speech and still rob every customer. Yahweh refuses the usual excuses (thin margins, competitors, pressure) and names the real cause: he loves to oppress (Hosea 12:7). Pressure can be relieved. An appetite has to be repented of. Here is how the verse shows it.
appr6-the-balances-of-deceit.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does Yahweh expose the appetite behind a dishonest trade? Because the deceit hides in the instrument, where a good impression never catches it, and because the root is not pressure but pleasure in getting the better of people (Hosea 12:7). Better circumstances cannot fix an appetite; only a different heart can. So build honest structures that catch what words cannot, and then look honestly inside, privately, for where the satisfaction of good work shades into enjoying someone else coming off worse.

teen.open: Can a scale lie without saying anything? Yes. A cheater can be friendly and still use a rigged scale. Yahweh says the real problem is not stress, but that he loves to take advantage.
teen.close: So why does Yahweh point at the heart? Because bad habits from pressure can be fixed with better times, but a love of cheating needs a changed heart.

senior.open: The title asks how a scale can lie without a word and why Yahweh exposes the appetite behind it. In Hosea 12:7 the deceit sits in the instrument, and the cause named is not pressure but a love of oppressing.
senior.close: So the answer is this. Structures catch what pleasant speech conceals, and Yahweh names the appetite because it is the true root. Circumstances can relieve pressure; an appetite must be located and repented of.

appr8-what-profit-shall-this-birthright-.reason: Builds Esau's scene for half the lesson before stating its answer (a valuation made in an extreme state prices the state, not the asset); ends on Isaiah 55 and the whole course, not on valuing your property.
appr8-what-profit-shall-this-birthright-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Esau's bowl of stew teach about valuing your own property? That a valuation made in a strong state, hungry, tired, hurt or afraid, prices the state and not the thing. Esau's arithmetic was sound. His input was wrong: he thought he was dying when he was hungry. So before you price something lasting, check the state you are in. Here is how Genesis 25 shows it.
appr8-what-profit-shall-this-birthright-.example: THE UNOPENED ENVELOPE. Say you have owned a small property for years. One evening an unwelcome envelope arrives, you sleep badly, and a buyer calls the next morning. Selling now feels urgent and obviously right. Nothing about the property changed overnight. Your state did. The lesson's counsel is to name that state first and let it pass before you put a number on something you cannot get back.
appr8-what-profit-shall-this-birthright-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Esau's stew teach about valuing your property? Hungry men do not price well. Esau sold something lasting to relieve something immediate, and the Word calls it despising his birthright (Genesis 25:34). Your state does not have to be dramatic to do your arithmetic for you; tiredness or a hard conversation will do. Jeremiah shows the other road, buying something lasting on Yahweh's word while everything immediate argued against it (Jeremiah 32:25). Know your state, then price the asset.

teen.open: What does Esau trading his birthright for stew teach about pricing your stuff? When you are hungry, tired or upset, you price your feelings, not the thing.
teen.close: So what's the lesson? Don't make big money decisions while you're upset or desperate. Notice your mood first, then decide.

senior.open: The title asks what Esau's bowl of stew teaches about valuing your own property. Genesis 25 shows that a valuation made in an extreme state prices the state, not the asset.
senior.close: So the answer holds. Esau's reasoning was sound but his input was false, and he traded the lasting for the immediate. Before valuing anything permanent, name your own state; Jeremiah bought the lasting thing on Yahweh's word.

appr7-the-worth-of-it-in-money.reason: Rightly spends time on Ahab's fair offer, but the answer (Naboth knew it was not for sale; Ahab only asked what is it worth) is the mid-lesson hinge; ends on Ahab's silent walk to the vineyard.
appr7-the-worth-of-it-in-money.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What did Naboth know that Ahab never asked? Ahab asked what the vineyard was worth, and his offer was fair, even generous. Naboth knew it was not for sale: it was the inheritance of his fathers. Those are two different questions, and a better price can never answer the second one. The question before what is it worth is: is it for sale at all? Here is how 1 Kings 21 shows it.
appr7-the-worth-of-it-in-money.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What did Naboth know that Ahab never asked? That some things are not for sale. Ahab's offer was fair (1 Kings 21:2), and nothing here makes fair offers wrong. But he only ever asked about price, so when Naboth refused, the problem had to be the seller, and Jezebel's telling makes it all a failed deal (1 Kings 21:15). Before you ask what something is worth, ask whether it is for sale. Then a refusal is an answer to respect, not an obstacle to manage.

teen.open: Ahab made a fair offer for Naboth's vineyard. So what did he miss? He asked how much it was worth, but never asked if it was for sale.
teen.close: So what did Naboth know? Some things are not for sale, even at a fair price. Ask that first, and respect a no.

senior.open: The title asks what Naboth knew that Ahab never asked. Ahab asked only what the vineyard was worth; Naboth knew it was his fathers' inheritance and not for sale.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. Ahab's offer was fair, yet it answered the wrong question. When every refusal is treated as a pricing problem, the seller becomes an obstacle. Ask first whether a thing is for sale.
